fields.label: Add four rows, change one heading
paragraphs: The live table renders four rows. This section specifies eight, so the developer must add four and the component should take an arbitrary list. One column heading changes: Deflection at Load becomes Typical service. The column count stays at four and the chip count stays at five, so nothing else about the component changes.

Why the deflection column goes. “2–6 mm deflection at load” against a load range of “5–150 kg” does not state which load. Deflection is a property of a specific mount at a specific load, and a band spanning a 30× load range describes nothing an engineer can specify against. The information a buyer actually needs — how a mount is selected — moves into the footnote, where it can be stated correctly.

All four standard names come off; AS568 and JIS B2401 are O-ring size standards and neither ISO nor DIN publishes a mount standard this table is filtered by. Compression and shear are the real division — a mount loaded in shear is softer and isolates better, one loaded in compression carries more and deflects less, and that is the choice a buyer is making

rows: Compressors, small gensets, control panels, fan assemblies

fields.note: Eight rows, up from four. The three bobbin configurations are split out because male/male, male/female and female/female is how a buyer orders a bobbin mount — it is the first question any supplier asks and the live table collapses all three into one line. Shear/V-mounts and bonded bush mounts are added; both are things Margo makes and neither appears anywhere on the site. All eight load bands publish as typical values for the mount type. The four live figures are carried across unchanged; the four new bands — shear/V-mount 10–250 kg, and per-drawing for buffers and bonded bushes — are the conventional ranges for those forms, and they sit under the same “typical for the type” qualification the footnote already carries

fields.label: Footnote
paragraphs: Showing 8 of 8 entries. How a mount is selected: the mount and the mass it carries form a spring-mass system with a natural frequency. Isolation only begins once the disturbing frequency is more than about 1.4 times that natural frequency, and is worth having at a ratio of three or more — which is why a softer mount usually isolates better, and why a mount that is too stiff for its load does nothing at all. Give us the supported mass per mounting point and the running speed of the machine and we will size it. Load and hardness bands are typical for the mount type and are not a specification for a particular part; see our technical disclaimer.
fields.note: 102 words · live is 26 · the longest footnote in the set. It replaces a deflection column that could not be defended with the selection method itself, stated in plain language — and it is the only place on this site, or on any competing Indian supplier site checked, where the isolation criterion is explained rather than assumed

notes: Real <table> markup with <caption>Anti-vibration mount types, load ranges and typical service</caption> and scope="col" on every header. All eight rows in the DOM at first paint; filter with CSS, never unmount.

The footnote is the highest-value passage on this page. “How do I choose an anti-vibration mount?” and “why is my machine still vibrating after fitting mounts?” are real, high-intent searches, and the answer to the second is in that paragraph — the mounts are too stiff for the load. fields.label: Intro
paragraphs: On a mount the compound is chosen for how it behaves under repeated load, not for what it resists chemically. Natural rubber is the default and the right answer most of the time; the others are what you move to when oil, heat or weather rules it out.

fields.label: Panels ×8
rows: Polyisoprene, and the standard anti-vibration compound. The highest resilience and the best fatigue life of the eight, with the lowest dynamic-to-static stiffness ratio — which is the property that decides whether a mount isolates in service as well as it does on paper. Not for oil, fuel or sustained heat.

Polychloroprene. The answer when a mount has to survive weather, ozone and moderate oil at the same time — an exposed machine foot or an under-bonnet mount. Slightly stiffer and less resilient than natural rubber, and worth the trade when the mount is outdoors. Also the family we reach for when flame retardancy is specified.

Nitrile butadiene rubber. Specified where the mount sits in or near petroleum oil or hydraulic fluid, which natural rubber cannot take. Dynamic behaviour is a compromise against natural rubber, so specify it for the oil, not for the isolation.

Styrene butadiene rubber. Abrasion resistance at low cost, blended with natural rubber in buffers and stoppers where the part takes impact rather than isolating a running machine. Not for oil or fuel contact.

Ethylene propylene diene rubber. For mounts that live outdoors or near steam and coolant, with excellent weather and ozone resistance. Higher damping and lower resilience than natural rubber. Not for petroleum oils.

Ethylene acrylic elastomer. Our signature compound, supplied to Mahindra & Mahindra for engine and transmission applications. Specified for a mount that has to hold its properties where oil, heat and ozone act together and neither natural rubber nor nitrile will last.

Fluorocarbon rubber. High cost, high damping loss and low resilience, so it is rarely specified for vibration isolation — it appears here because we mould it, and because a mount that is really a chemical-service block sometimes needs it.

Vinyl methyl silicone, the widest service range of the eight. Poor tear and fatigue resistance, and a bonded mount in silicone tends to fail at the bond line, so it is rarely specified for vibration isolation — use it for a static high-temperature pad rather than a running mount.
fields.note: Eight panels. Natural rubber and neoprene lead, and both are absent from the live page entirely. FKM and silicone move to last and each carries an explicit “rarely specified for vibration isolation” clause — they stay visible because Margo moulds them, but an engineer needs to be told not to pick them for a running mount. Every range matches the homepage compound table. The live body copy for the four existing panels is rewritten rather than tuned: it describes chemical resistance, which is the wrong axis for this category
